section.title: Related rates
section.p: Some quantities change alone. Many do not.
If a balloon is being inflated, its radius changes, its surface area changes, and its volume changes. These quantities are linked. Knowing how fast one changes can tell us how fast another changes.
That is the idea of a related rates problem.
The bridge is the chain rule.

exercise.title: Why does an equation relating quantities become an equation relating rates?

statement.p: If two quantities are linked by a formula that remains true as time passes, the chain rule turns that formula into a relation among derivatives. In your own words, why is that the idea of a related rates problem, and why must we remember that each quantity is secretly a function of time?

hint.p: An equation relating quantities implies an equation relating their rates. The bridge is the chain rule, not a new kind of derivative.

exercise.title: Why must we differentiate before substituting the values of one instant?

statement.p: The numbers x=6 and y=8 describe one snapshot of x^2+y^2=100. Differentiating after substituting them yields only 0=0. In your own words, why does that destroy the rate information, and what is the difference between the changing variables and the numbers that describe one moment?

hint.p: First differentiate the relation that remains true over time. Then plug in the values known at the instant in question.

subsection.title: Geometry problems: ladders, shadows, cones
subsection.p: Geometry supplies many clean related rates problems because lengths, areas, and volumes are linked by familiar formulas.

note.title: A rate is not just a number
note.p: A rate carries units and direction. Before trusting an answer, ask:
note.md: \text{Was the equation differentiated before instant-specific values were substituted?}

subsection.p: Related rates tell how quantities change together. The next problem is different. Instead of asking how fast something changes, we ask which choice is best.

exercise.title: Why is a rate not just a number?

statement.p: A related-rates answer carries units and a sign. In your own words, why do matching units catch many algebra mistakes, and why does a positive \frac{dy}{dt} for a ladder sliding down the wall mean the labels, not the calculus, have gone wrong?

hint.p: Before trusting an answer, ask whether the sign makes sense and whether the units make sense. A rate remembers direction as well as size.
